Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event
Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same node's strong intrusive, poorly controlled re-experiencing items ('triggered without warning' and 'full sensory reliving'). Severe reliving can coexist with disclosure, but 'very easily' pulls in the opposite direction and is the clearest within-node inconsistency.

issues.item: Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation leaves Threat disconnected from the active network, yet 'Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time' implies a strong ongoing sense of current threat. That threat-focused appraisal is not supported by the formulation and is not matched by any Threat-node content.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: 'Entrapment: Having no options' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The negative appraisals and memory content center on global damage/self-reliance and sensory reliving, not on themes of being trapped or unable to escape, so this trigger appears insufficiently grounded in the reported formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The triggers and appraisals do not indicate body-strain or exertion as a salient trauma-linked theme, making this strategy look disconnected from the reported trigger-memory-appraisal pattern.

The trigger profile is centered on entrapment, touch, and a specific taste, which implies reactivity to concrete sensory or situational reminders of the witnessed trauma. 'Entrapment: Having no options' is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile because the memory and appraisal items do not describe being trapped or immobilized; they emphasize sensory reliving, nonverbal memory, hypervigilance, and global damage/self-doubt rather than a trapped-state theme. For a witnessed-trauma case, this item stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The selected triggers and memory items point to sensory cue-driven reliving, and the appraisals concern vigilance, self-reliance, and life damage. Avoiding bodily stress suggests fear of physiological arousal or somatic activation, but there are no corresponding threat or appraisal items about bodily danger, losing control when activated, or physical collapse. It therefore looks like a maladaptive strategy targeting a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Reminders' appears mis-keyed: the strategy should be an avoidant behavior (e.g., avoiding being reminded), but the selected text describes a trigger/reminder rather than something the patient does. This makes the maladaptive-strategy item internally incoherent.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The profile includes a prominent current-threat appraisal ('I have to be on guard all the time') despite Threat being structurally inactive: there are no active edges to or from Threat, and the rest of the profile is dominated by memory-based reexperiencing, negative self-appraisals, and coping strategies rather than an active external-danger formulation. This item fits Threat more than Negative Appraisals and is inconsistent with the specified formulation.

vignette:
For eighteen months, the accident had lived inside him without words. Mark could not have described what he saw that afternoon even if he had wanted to, and he did not want to. He was a carpenter, thirty years old, married, steady—or he had been. The job site was a three-story frame-up on the edge of town, and he was on the ground floor running trim when the foreman yelled. Mark looked up just as a co-worker named Derek lost his footing on a ladder propped against an open second-floor joist. Derek fell sideways, his head catching the edge of a concrete footer on the way down. The sound was wet and wrong. Mark dropped his nail gun and ran over. He was the first one there. Derek was on his back, blood pooling under his skull, his eyes open but not tracking. Mark knelt and reached out without thinking, his hand finding Derek’s shoulder, then Derek’s fingers curling around his wrist with a grip that felt like desperation. The metallic taste of his own blood flooded Mark’s mouth—he had bitten his tongue hard when the body hit the ground, and he had not even noticed until that moment. He stayed there, frozen, until the paramedics pulled him away.

In the weeks that followed, Mark found he could not talk about it. When his wife, Carrie, asked what happened, he said “I saw something bad” and then stopped, because the words were not there. What was there instead was the sensation of Derek’s hand on his wrist, a phantom pressure he could not shake. He started wearing long sleeves even in summer, and he flinched when Carrie touched his arm. He stopped eating lunch in the break trailer because the taste of the sandwich he had been eating—turkey with mustard—now arrived without warning in his mouth whenever he saw a drop of blood on a bandage or a scrape on a child’s knee. And the worst part was that he could not control when the memory came. It would slam into him while he was measuring a piece of lumber: the full sensory replay—the crack, the weight of Derek’s hand, the copper taste, the red pooling on gray concrete—all of it alive again, as if time had folded. He would stand frozen, heart pounding, until he could force his mind to go somewhere else. He learned to do that deliberately. When the wave started, he would imagine his body emptying out, becoming a shell, nothing inside. He would stare at a point on the wall and feel himself drift upward, blank and weightless. It worked, mostly, but it left him exhausted.

Food became his other escape. At night, after Carrie had gone to bed, Mark would sit in the kitchen and eat whatever was in the pantry—cereal, crackers, frozen pizza—mechanically, until his stomach ached. Eating dulled the edge of the dread that lived in his chest. He gained nearly thirty pounds over the year, and Carrie started making comments about his health. He knew she was worried, but he could not explain that he was trying to kill something inside himself with every bite.

On the job site, Mark had become a different carpenter. He could not trust himself to work on scaffolding anymore. He would check and recheck the locks, and even then his hands would shake. His foreman noticed and moved him to ground-level work, which meant fewer hours and less pay. Mark told himself it was temporary, but deep down he believed he had permanently changed for the worse. He was certain his life had been destroyed by that single afternoon. He used to think of himself as capable, someone who could handle anything. Now he felt like a stranger in his own body—someone who could not rely on himself to stay present, to eat normally, to let his wife touch him. The worst thought came in the quiet moments: I am broken, and I will never be fixed.

What finally brought Mark to the clinic was a Tuesday evening when he came home from a half-day of work, avoided Carrie’s goodbye kiss, ate an entire bag of chips without tasting them, and then sat on the couch trying to disappear from his own mind. Carrie sat down across from him and said, quietly, “You are not here. You haven’t been here in a year. I don’t know who you are anymore.” Mark looked at her, and for a moment he wanted to tell her everything—the taste, the touch, the way he had to leave his body to survive the day—but the words would not come. So he just nodded. The next morning, he called the number on the card she had left on the counter. He did not know if talking could help. He was afraid it might make things worse, that describing the event would bring it back fully and he would never return. But he was more afraid of losing his wife, of losing the last thread that tied him to the man he used to be. So he came, sat in the chair, and waited to see if there was any way back.
